transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Recording: auto

Summary: quick intake call to understand SkyForge's latency and throughput targets for a new agent chat feature that will be used in customer support workflows. They want guidance on whether Hosted, Dedicated, or Private makes sense given p95 goals and burst behavior around release windows.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side, with Luca our Solutions Engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Derek Hayes: Good, thanks. Sorry ran a minute behind.
[00:08] Priya Nambiar: Hi, Priya here. Running the model infra team.
[00:10] Carlos Mendez: Carlos, SRE. We'll talk failure scenarios.
[00:13] Luca Ramos: Great. Quick agenda — gather current stack, p95 targets, concurrency, streaming requirements, and then propose a benchmarking plan.
[00:20] Derek: Yeah, top line — we're building an in-product agent that streams responses back to users. Target p95 for token streaming end-to-end ideally under 200ms on the last token for short prompts, and p95 under 400ms for longer 512-token responses. Burst concurrency — 3k concurrent streaming sessions during major releases, sustained 300-400 concurrent.
[00:40] Maya: That's helpful. Do you have a current tokens/sec baseline from your PoC?
[00:44] Priya: We ran a small test using a hosted provider — we saw about 1.8k tokens/sec aggregate from a single instance at low sequence lengths, but latencies were spiky at peak, p95 ballooned to 900ms during bursts.
[00:58] Luca: Ok spike is typical without batching and KV cache tuned. Quick question on KV cache usage: do you persist conversational state server-side or rely on prefix windows?
[01:06] Priya: We keep a small rolling history in Redis, but the real KV cache is in-process on the model server in the PoC. We haven't implemented prefix caching across requests.
[01:15] Carlos: Our ops concern is cold starts and scale-up time. We don't want 5–10s tail latencies when traffic ramps during a flash sale.
[01:23] Maya: Understood. For clarity, when you say Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private — Hosted is Redwood-managed multi-tenant endpoints, Dedicated is reserved GPU pools for only SkyForge, Private is VPC/air-gapped. Which are you leaning to?
[01:35] Derek: We like the dev speed of Hosted but nervous about predictable p95 during peaks. Private seems heavy ops-wise. Dedicated might be middle ground but cost is a concern.
[01:44] Luca: That's a common tradeoff. Dedicated gives you predictable concurrency and no noisy neighbor interference; Hosted can be tuned with reserved capacity or burst policies. Private gives full control over network and KMS but requires ops investment.
[01:58] Priya: Can you quantify typical p95s for streaming on Hosted for, say, a 70B-like open model with Redwood streaming?
[02:06] Luca: Ballpark — on hosted with the standard profile and dynamic batching it's common to see streaming p95 between 120–220ms for short prompts at medium concurrency. For longer outputs p95 climbs; with dedicated and tuned KV cache you can bring it down compared to multi-tenant. But exact numbers depend on sequence distribution and batching window.
[02:28] Derek: What about tokens/sec throughput per card — we need to understand how many GPUs for our 3k burst.
[02:34] Luca: For 70B family quantized runtimes, rough token/sec per GPU is in the 8k–16k tokens/sec range depending on token length and whether you use int8 quantization or not. So for a 3k concurrent streaming scenario you need to model average tokens generated per session, token/sec per session, and concurrency.
[02:55] Maya: If helpful, we can run a comparative pilot: 24h replay of your traffic on Hosted vs Dedicated to show p95 delta and cost. It catches tail behavior and ramp characteristics.
[03:05] Priya: That would be really useful. Are there additional instrumentation hooks we need to add to our traces?
[03:10] Luca: Ideally include per-request timestamps for request start, first byte, last byte, and per-token timings if possible. If not, a replay with correct inter-arrival times plus the prompt/payloads will suffice.
[03:21] Carlos: Security — we need to know about KMS integration, encryption at rest, and audit logs. Also SSO, RBAC.
[03:28] Maya: Redwood supports KMS integration for Private and Dedicated. Hosted uses our managed key but we offer Bring-Your-Own-Key for Dedicated/Private; we also have audit logs and SAML SSO/RBAC. I'll attach the security pack.
[03:36] Derek: Do you support on-prem private? We have some regulated customers that require air-gapped options.
[03:40] Luca: Yes we have an on-prem/private distribution and VPC-private control plane for customers that need it; that's higher operational overhead but gives you full data residency and network control.
[03:48] Priya: Latency within their network — if we go Private on-prem, we'd likely be closer to users so network latency will help. But our team is small and we don't want to run all of the infra.
[03:58] Maya: Right. For acceptance criteria, what are your must-haves? You mentioned p95 numbers earlier, anything else?
[04:05] Derek: Must-haves: p95 last-token streaming < 200ms for short flows, <400ms for long flows; no more than 5% error rate on token streaming; scaling ramp under 30s for doubling traffic; cost target under $0.0008 per token at steady-state — ballpark.
[04:24] Luca: Cost target is tight but we can model simulated numbers. One lever is batching window; more aggressive batching reduces token cost but increases latency. Also prefix/KV caching reduces computation for repeated contexts.
[04:35] Carlos: How does Redwood handle fallback if a model variant is out of capacity mid-flow? Do you have streaming fallbacks?
[04:41] Luca: We do model variant fallback rules and region failover. For streaming, best practice is to have a fast smaller model for first N tokens and a higher-quality fallback, or a degraded streaming mode that returns incremental text with slightly higher latency but preserves availability. We can configure automatic fallback policies.
[05:00] Priya: We run a multi-tenant PoC on another provider and saw p95 regressions during global experiments. Curious if Redwood provides QoS or traffic shaping to prioritize critical tokens.
[05:10] Maya: For Dedicated and Private you can define routing policies and QoS tiers; for Hosted we offer reserved capacity and can do priority pools for critical production routes.
[05:19] Derek: Ok let's talk concrete benchmarking. What do you need from us to run the 24h replay?
[05:24] Luca: Sample traces with timestamps, request payloads (redact user PII), desired concurrency schedule for the 24h window, and success criteria. We'll run the same replay against Hosted baseline and a Dedicated reservation sized per your expected peak. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 for first-byte, per-token, and last-byte, plus error/retry rates and memory/cold-start stats.
[05:46] Priya: We can sanitize and produce a CSV. We also have a synthetic script that generates sessions; would that be ok?
[05:50] Luca: Yes synthetic is fine as long as it mimics inter-arrival and sequence length distribution. If you can provide a small sample of real traces that will tune the generator.
[05:58] Carlos: Will you run a quantized variant test? We rely on int8 quant for cost reasons.
[06:03] Luca: Yes we can test int8 quantized runtimes and unquantized. We'll include model variants used in the PoC. Note quantization slightly changes latency profile and sometimes quality — we can capture that.
[06:16] Derek: Any special network or firewall rules we need to open for Dedicated?
[06:20] Maya: For Dedicated you'll have a customer-dedicated endpoint and we can provide IP ranges for allowlist. For Private/VPC we'll need peering or VPN config. I'll share the ops doc.
[06:28] Priya: One more thing — streaming fragmentation. Our client expects chunked events with stable ordering; do you guarantee ordering and acks?
[06:36] Luca: Streaming is done over HTTP/2 or websockets depending on your integration; we maintain per-session ordering and can provide sequence metadata to detect missing chunks. We also have retry strategies for transient errors.
[06:48] Derek: Great. On the billing side, if we do Dedicated reserved capacity, what's typical commit sizing and scale-up options?
[06:55] Maya: Commits start monthly for a number of GPUs; we have auto-burst credits and overage tiers. We'll share the committed capacity worksheet. There's flexibility to adjust after the initial quarter.
[07:06] Carlos: Regarding observability, do you provide per-route token/latency breakdowns and traces?
[07:11] Luca: Yes Console provides per-route and per-model breakdowns, sample traces, and token-level cost breakdown. You can integrate our tracing hooks with OpenTelemetry.
[07:20] Derek: Ok sounds good. Can you share an example benchmark report from a previous customer?
[07:24] Maya: I'll attach a redacted benchmarking report showing p95 deltas between Hosted and Dedicated, along with cost per token.
[07:30] Priya: For success criteria — can we agree to a follow-up meeting after pilot to decide hosting mode, with a timeline to pick production by end of June?
[07:37] Maya: Yes we'll target the week of June 15–19 for the deep-dive.
[07:41] Derek: That works.
[07:43] Luca: Quick clarifying Q — you mentioned 3k concurrent sessions at burst. What's average tokens per session during a burst event?
[07:49] Priya: Average about 120 tokens per session, but some sessions hit 400 tokens. Most traffic is short — a lot of 30–90 token exchanges.
[07:58] Luca: Ok that helps sizing. We'll model two scenarios: short-heavy and long-tail.
[08:03] Maya: Anything else we should capture?
[08:05] Carlos: Failover RTO — if a region goes down, how long to shift to another region for streaming without major user-visible gaps?
[08:12] Luca: With warm warmups and cross-region replication you can be sub-30s for most traffic; fully cold failover can be longer. We recommend cross-region warm pools for critical flows.
[08:23] Derek: One last item — compliance: SOC2 attestation timeline and certifications for Dedicated/Private?
[08:29] Maya: We have SOC2 Type II and ISO catalog; for Private deployments we can provide compliance artifacts and engage security onboarding.
[08:36] Priya: Cool. We'll prepare traces and the replay script.
[08:39] Derek: Perfect. Thanks.
[08:41] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the worksheet and next steps.

Notes on transcript quality: a few misheard acronyms: "KV cache" recorded as "K V cash" in some timestamps, some punctuation missing, speaker turns overlap occasionally.

End of transcript.
